notes:
I found traditional commentary on most verses. I couldn't find anything usable on vv. 13, 15–18 and 20, so I left them out. On v. 11 I have only a short opening. My searches didn't reach netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org or oca.org, and I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this passage, so those parts are missing. The tradition labels on older commentators (Gill as Baptist, Clarke as Methodist, and so on) are mine; the pages themselves don't give them.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:** Luke is writing real history, not "once upon a time." Augustus, the "political savior" of a war-torn world, was only a tool God used to get Mary to Bethlehem, as Micah 5:2 foretold. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/
- **Traditional reading:** Matthew Henry says the timing was fitting. Rome ruled almost the whole known world, which Henry links to Daniel 2:44, and the empire was at peace, a fitting moment for the Prince of Peace to be born. https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC42002.HTM

**v. 2**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says the census was for tax purposes. Luke calls it the "first" to set it apart from the better-known census of A.D. 6 (Acts 5:37). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/
- **The historical problem:** Barnes calls this one of the most puzzling verses in the New Testament, because Quirinius was not governor of Syria until 12 to 15 years after Jesus' birth. Barnes https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lsv/luke/2-2.html
- **Proposed solutions:**
  - Clarke suggests Augustus sent Quirinius into Syria with special powers to carry out this census before he was formally governor. Clarke https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lsv/luke/2-2.html
  - Gill similarly says he was sent to Judea for this registration, which was separate from the later one under his governorship. Gill https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/luke/2-2.html
  - Ellicott reads the verse as "the first enrolment under Quirinius's government," distinguishing it from the census Gamaliel mentions in Acts 5:37. Ellicott https://biblehub.com/luke/2-2.htm
- **Critical view (the closest I found to modern scholarship):** A Bible Hub article reports that secular historians date Quirinius's formal governorship to A.D. 6–9, a decade after Jesus was born under Herod. It then defends Luke's accuracy, for example by pointing to an inscription many scholars take to describe Quirinius governing twice. The defence https://biblehub.com/q/Luke_2_2_vs_Quirinius_census_history.htm

**v. 3**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says one man gave an order and the world obeyed, yet his power was given from above (John 19:10–11). Secular records don't preserve the order to return to ancestral towns, but it fits what is known of Augustus, and Barclay cites a similar census edict from Egypt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/

**v. 4**
- **Traditional reading:** The trip was about 80 miles, a serious undertaking. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/
- **Traditional reading:** Henry notes that Bethlehem means "house of bread," fitting for the Bread of life. He also says the census records proved Jesus was of David's line, and that Justin Martyr and Tertullian appealed to them. https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC42002.HTM

**v. 5**
- **Traditional reading:** Mary may not have been required to go. Guzik, citing Liefeld, suggests Joseph may have used the journey to take her away from gossip in Nazareth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/

**v. 6**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says Mary was not necessarily close to delivery when they set out. The birth happened "while they were there." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/

**v. 7** (the most disputed verse)
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Luke tells huge events very simply. "Swaddling cloths" may come from a word meaning "to tear" (Trapp). Justin Martyr placed the birth in a cave. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/
  - Henry says the inn and manger show the family's poverty and Christ's humility, and that Christ came only to "sojourn" here. https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC42002.HTM
  - Barclay pictures an eastern khan, with the birth taking place in its common courtyard. Barclay https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/2-7.html
- **Disagreement over "firstborn":**
  - **Other children:** Guzik says the word invites the logical conclusion that Mary had other children, "despite the Roman Catholic teaching." Guzik https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/ Barnes agrees that this is the obvious meaning. Barnes The Light of Israel commentary goes further, saying the word itself shows later siblings. Light of Israel https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/2-7.html
  - **Not necessarily:** Gill (a Baptist) says "firstborn" meant the first to open the womb, even if no others followed (Exodus 13:2). Gill https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/2-7.html
  - **Calvin:** In a Catholic Answers debate, Trent Horn states that Calvin did not believe in Mary's perpetual virginity. This is Horn's claim; I did not see it in Calvin's own text. Horn https://www.catholic.com/audio/cot/debate-do-the-marian-dogmas-contradict-scripture-with-steve-christie
- **Catholic view:**
  - Catholic Answers argues the word is at best ambiguous. Luke quotes the law on the firstborn (Exodus 13:2) in the same chapter, so "firstborn" means "first to open the womb." Catholic Answers An ambiguous text cannot overturn the historic belief. Catholic Answers https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/firstborn-jesus-brothers-and-sisters
  - Jerome (A.D. 383) argued that a son with no younger brothers was still bound by the law of the firstborn. Jerome https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3007.htm

**v. 8**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says Bethlehem's shepherds may have tended the temple's sacrificial flocks. He also says the shepherds being outdoors does not rule out a December date. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/
- **Traditional reading:** Henry notes the angel went to humble shepherds, not chief priests. They were awake and at their honest work, which shows we are "not out of the way of divine visits" in an honest calling. https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC42002.HTM

**v. 9**
- **Traditional reading:** Henry says the angel "stood over them" unexpectedly. Their fear reflects guilty consciences dreading a message of wrath. https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC42002.HTM

**v. 10**
- **Traditional reading:** "I bring good tidings" literally means the angel preached the gospel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/
- **Traditional reading:** Henry says the joy is for all people, "not to the people of the Jews only." https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC42002.HTM

**v. 11**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik's devotional says that, like Mary, believers hear God say His Son is "Christ the Lord, Messiah and God." Guzik https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/what-mary-knew/

**v. 12**
- **Traditional reading:** Henry says the manger's lowliness is balanced by the angels' glory: "Surely it can be no other than the Son of God." https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC42002.HTM

**v. 14** (wording and tradition differences)
- **Traditional reading:** Ellicott says the better manuscripts read "peace among men of good will," meaning the people who receive God's approval and love. Ellicott https://biblehub.com/luke/2-14.htm
- **Evangelical view:** Constable calls the KJV's "good will toward men" misleading, because it could suggest God's favour rests on human merit. Constable https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/2-14.html
- **Tradition differences:**
  - **Gill (Baptist, Calvinist):** God's special good will is toward "elect men," not all men. Gill https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/2-14.html
  - **Calvin:** Either reading works. He says the peace "takes effect only when we receive it," and that God has shown undeserved favour to men once at war with Him. Calvin https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/2-14.html
  - **Bengel (Lutheran):** The word means God's newly revealed favour "towards the whole human race." Bengel https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/2-14.htm
  - **Clarke (Methodist):** People reconciled to God gain peace with God, with their own consciences and with their neighbours. Clarke https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/luke/2-14.html
  - **Spurgeon:** He preaches the KJV reading and urges, "Do not try to celebrate Christmas without keeping good will towards men." Spurgeon https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/2-14.html
- **Modern evangelical view:** A Gospel Coalition writer says God gives peace not to everyone, but to those who have His favour. TGC https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/article/peace-among-those-with-whom-he-is-pleased-and-just-who-is-that/

**v. 19**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says Mary treasured the shepherds' report with affection. After nine silent months, angels were again at work, recalling Gabriel's visit. Guzik https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/what-mary-knew/

**v. 21**
- **Traditional reading:** The circumcision probably took place at home, not the temple, following Genesis 17 and Leviticus 12:3, and the naming went with it. "Jesus" (Jeshua) means "the Lord is salvation." The author suggests the name helped Simeon recognize Him ("mine eyes have seen Thy salvation"). https://bible.org/seriespage/5-psalm-simeon-and-announcement-anna-luke-221-40

**v. 22** (tradition differences)
- **Traditional reading:** There were three separate rites: circumcision, presentation and purification. Purification came about 40 days after a son's birth, so Jesus was about six weeks old. https://bible.org/seriespage/5-psalm-simeon-and-announcement-anna-luke-221-40
- **What "their purification" means:**
  - **Guzik:** The better reading is "*their* purification." The rites remind us that we are all born in sin, and Jesus "was identified with sinners even as a baby." Guzik https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-2/
  - **Constable:** Ritual uncleanness was not sin. Mary's uncleanness came from childbirth and shows Jesus was truly human. Constable https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/2-22.html
  - **Gill:** Mary was not polluted by bearing Jesus, but was unclean in the eyes of the law. Gill https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/2-22.html
- **Catholic vs Protestant:** In a Catholic Answers debate, Protestant Steve Christie argues that Mary's offerings under Leviticus 12 show she needed atonement, which he says is unnecessary if she were immaculately conceived. Christie https://www.catholic.com/audio/cot/debate-do-the-marian-dogmas-contradict-scripture-with-steve-christie

**v. 23**
- **Traditional reading:** The firstborn belonged to God because Israel's firstborn were spared at the Passover. The redemption price was five shekels (Numbers 18:16). https://bible.org/seriespage/5-psalm-simeon-and-announcement-anna-luke-221-40
- **Catholic view:** Catholic Answers notes this redemption was required for every first son, whether or not a second ever followed. Catholic Answers https://www.catholic.com/audio/ddp/jesus-as-firstborn

**v. 24**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Clarke: one bird was a burnt offering and one a sin offering. Two birds instead of a lamb show the family was poor. Clarke
  - Calvin: the sacrifice belonged to Mary's purification, not to redeeming the firstborn. Calvin
  - Barnes: Christ's poverty shows it is not dishonourable to be poor. Barnes
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/2-24.html

**v. 25**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Barnes: "consolation of Israel" was a common title for the coming Messiah, and Jews even swore by it. Barnes
  - Ellicott: the Spirit being upon him points to a special moment of inspiration rather than constant guidance. Ellicott
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the Spirit was returning after nearly 400 years of absence. JFB
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/2-25.htm
- **Who was Simeon?** The Pulpit Commentary mentions an old theory that he was Hillel's son, but calls it "very precarious." Pulpit https://biblehub.com/luke/2-25.htm
- **Traditional reading:** Calvin says such hope was rare, so few in that age truly looked for redemption. Calvin Constable notes the text does not actually say Simeon was old. Constable https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/2-25.html
- **Reformed Baptist view:** John Piper says Luke repeats this "waiting" theme (v. 25 and v. 38) because longing for God to act is what made Simeon and Anna ready to recognize Christ. Piper https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/preparing-to-receive-christ-looking-for-the-consolation-of-israel

**v. 26**
- **Traditional reading:** The Spirit revealed the promise, led Simeon to the temple and showed him which child it was. Luke cares more that a Spirit-filled man identified Jesus as the Lord's Christ than about how he knew. https://bible.org/seriespage/5-psalm-simeon-and-announcement-anna-luke-221-40
- **Traditional reading:** Henry says Christ is not only the giver of comfort but its very substance, "the consolation of Israel," and is worth waiting for. Henry https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC42002.HTM
